subtopic: STANDING ORDER NO. 60  SPEAKER'S RULING
STANDING ORDER NO. 60  SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
Probably I might at this time give my ruling with respect to standing order No. 60.
On May 20 the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) requested me to consider standing order No. 60 and to give my opinion as to its proper construction. On June 4 and
1. No.

16 there were further discussions on this standing order, which reads as follows:
If any motion be made in the house for any public aid or charge upon the people, the consideration and debate thereof may not be presently entered upon, but shall be adjourned till such further day as the house thinks fit to appoint: and then it shall be referred to a committee of the whole house, before any resolution or vote of the house do pass thereupon.
All hon. members who have taken part in the discussions agree that the motion that the Speaker do leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole to consider a resolution preceding a money-bill is debatable. In my opinion that is the correct view so long as subclause (a) of standing order No. 38 remains in its present form.
The question on which there is some difference of opinion is the extent to which debate is to be allowed. This question was considered by Mr. Speaker Glen on the 23rd of February, 1942. At that time he ruled that the debate should be directed to the negative of the motion and should be general with no reference to details.
I should point out that the motion is for the Speaker to leave the chair, etc. It is not a motion to adopt the resolution. However, under our present practice members have been debating it as if it were such a motion. The minister makes an affirmative statement, frequently going into details, with the Speaker in the chair, and other members follow. The result is that a full discussion of the resolution takes place at this stage. I am sure that Is not the procedure contemplated by standing order No. 60, nor is it in accordance with Mr. Speaker Glen's ruling, in which I concur.
After giving this matter my careful consideration I have come to the conclusion that if there is no objection to the consideration of the resolution in committee of the whole, the motion that the Speaker do leave the chair should be put without debate. If any members are opposed to the resolution, and do not think that it should even be considered in the committee of the whole, or if they require additional information before agreeing to the motion, they should be given an opportunity to speak on the motion. The minister should endeavour to answer the objections which have been raised and to give the information requested.
Accordingly in my opinion the practice of the minister opening the debate on the motion for the Speaker to leave the chair for the house to consider in committee of the whole a resolution preceding a money bill should be discontinued.
When the discussion on this subject was before the house the other night a number of members expressed concern over the difficulty
Business of the House which the Speaker would have in keeping the debate within the limits of the above interpretation. I realize the difficulty but all I can do is to ask for the usual co-operation of all hon. members.

subtopic: USE OF RADIOTELEPHONE ON GREAT LAKES- APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT

speakeroldname: Hon. Lionel Chevrier (Minister of Transport) moved:
subtopic: USE OF RADIOTELEPHONE ON GREAT LAKES- APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT
speechtext:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament approve the agreement for the promotion of safety on the great lakes by means of radio between Canada and the United States of America, signed at Ottawa, February 21, 1952, and that this house do approve the same.
He said: Mr. Speaker, at this stage I would like to table two copies of the agreement for the promotion of safety on the great lakes by means of radio. I understand the practice is to table those prior to discussion of the resolution.
The agreement referred to in the resolution has been under discussion and under consideration by Canada and the United States for some months. The purpose of the agreement is to provide for the safety of life on the great lakes by means of radiotelephone or the installation of radiotelephony equipment. This agreement will not come into force until two years after it has been ratified by both parties. It may be terminated after a period of five years, providing a notice of twelve months has been given. The agreement authorizes the use of radiotelephony as
3376	HOUSE OF
Promotion of Safety on Great Lakes a means of communication and for transmission of distress signals by ships on the great lakes, on the distress frequency of 2182 kilocycles and the continuance of the present working frequencies. It provides also for the compulsory installation of radiotelephone equipment on
(a)	All great lakes shipping of 500 gross tons and over.
(b)	All passenger carrying vessels over 65 feet in length.
(c)	On every vessel of less than 500 gross tons engaged in towing another vessel of 500 gross tons or over or any floating object having dimension of 150 feet or more, unless the towing vessel or object complies with the agreement.
The agreement further requires that a continuous listening watch be maintained on the distress frequency of 2182 kilocycles by all vessels that are subject to this agreement. It also stipulates that each government shall undertake to ensure that necessary arrangements are made for a listening watch by coast stations on that frequency. All of the provisions of the agreement apply to vessels subject thereto while they are being navigated on the great lakes or connecting channels such as the St. Mary's river, the St. Clair river, lake St. Clair, the Detroit river, the Welland ship canal and the river St. Lawrence as far east as the lower exit of the Lachine canal and the Victoria bridge at Montreal.
Provision is made in the agreement for the exclusion of various ships of war, such as destroyers, corvettes and the like, together with vessels in tow, vessels not self-propelled by mechanical means, government vessels not engaged in trade and certain others as specified in article 3. In general terms, as set forth in the preamble of the agreement, the purpose of the agreement is to promote safety of life and property on the great lakes of North America by means of radio, and especially to make provision for radiotelephone communication for safety purposes, including communication as an aid to navigation.
Basically, the agreement constitutes mutual recognition by the governments of the two countries that radiotelephony, which enables direct communication between vessels as well as from ship to shore, should be the primary means of promoting safety on the great lakes. Radiotelephony, as the house knows, is now used extensively and effectively on the great lakes as a means of aiding navigation and of securing assistance in time of distress. So far as radio is concerned, the great lakes presents specialized problems requiring special treatment based on local conditions. The peculiar requirements of the great lakes


have promoted a rapid development of ship-to-ship and ship-to-shore radio telephone communication. This has been a rapid and largely spontaneous development on the part of the shipping industry.
Technical regulations have been appended or annexed to the agreement which I tabled a moment ago, and it is provided in article 1 of the agreement that these regulations may be amended, as may be necessary, by agreement between the two governments. The house will have an opportunity of seeing the provisions of the agreement. I do not want to go into them at this stage in detail, but perhaps a general review will serve some purpose.
Article 1 of the agreement contains general provisions for the carrying out of the agreement and its applications to vessels of all countries.
Article 2 contains definitions of terms found in the agreement.
Article 3 defines the categories of vessels to which the agreement applies, and also those which are excluded from the application of the agreement.
Article 4 stipulates that a vessel which is not subject to the agreement does not become subject thereto due to stress of weather or force majeure.
Article 5 provides for the making of necessary arrangements for a listening watch by coast stations on the distress frequency.
Article 6 provides for exemption of vessels either partially, conditionally or completely from certain of the provisions of the agreement relating to technical operations.
Articles 7 to 14 inclusive contain provisions affecting technical operations, including those relating to operators, radiotelephone installation, vessel records, authority of the master, inspections and surveys, certification and privileges, issuance of certificate on request of responsible administration, and control.
Article 15 provides that the two governments, to the extent permitted by their respective constitutional procedures, will undertake to assist the vessels of other countries in meeting the requirements of the agreement.
Article 16 relates to the exchange of information respecting laws, regulations and reports.
Articles 17 and 18 provide for ratification, coming into force, duration and termination.
I should like to say just one word about the number of ships affected by this agreement. With respect to the number of vessels of Canadian registry which will be subject to the requirements of this agreement, I should like to point out that there are 221 cargo

vessels of 500 tons or over already fitted with radiotelephone and affected by this agreement, and 90 of those will require some improvement of their installations. This means that 131 vessels are now equipped with radiotelephony in accordance with the terms of the agreement. There are 19 passenger vessels over 65 feet in length affected by the agreement. Two require more up-to-date apparatus, and four will require to be fitted with the prescribed equipment. The very fact that so many operators voluntarily have equipped their vessels with radiotelephone installations is a clear indication of their preference for radiotelephony. It is considered the two-year period above-mentioned is ample time to permit adaptation to these regulations.
The implementation of this agreement will require an amendment to section 406 of the Canada Shipping Act, which is the governing section, to provide that ships subject to the agreement shall be fitted with a radiotelephone installation. It is the intention of the government to introduce at the next session of parliament an amendment to section 406 so as to make this provision of the agreement applicable. Perhaps here I could anticipate questions from the opposition as to whether or not this will be referred to a standing committee of the house. The government feels that that is not necessary at this time, in view of the statement which I have just made, because when the section is amended at the next session of parliament it will unquestionably be necessary to refer the whole of the agreement to a standing committee.
The obligations of the agreement will apply to ships on international voyages beginning or terminating on the great lakes or St. Lawrence river above Montreal, in addition to the obligations to which they are subject under the international convention for the safety of life at sea. The imposition of these additional obligations on ships in inland waters does not appear to conflict with the international safety convention. This agreement should work to the advantage of the safety convention ships using the great lakes and the St. Lawrence river above Montreal, as it will place at their disposal the extensive radiotelephone facilities which will be provided by coast stations and ships operating on the great lakes. Assistance will be given to foreign ships requiring such assistance by a depot established at Montreal where equipment will be available at low cost. It is expected that there will be only a minor demand for this equipment, inasmuch as vessels now plying on the great lakes from outside points are usually equipped with radiotelephone, or will be so equipped in the very near future with the adoption on a
Promotion of Safety on Great Lakes world-wide basis of the frequency of 2182 kilocycles for safety and distress radiotelephone communication.
The government has recognized for some time the need for an agreement with the United States dealing with the use of radio on the great lakes. This matter has been under consideration between the two countries for some years and the agreement which is the subject of this resolution has been carefully prepared by representatives of both countries. It has been received favourably by the shipping operators on the great lakes. The government considers that, if ratified by both countries, the agreement will be beneficial to shipping on the great lakes, and I recommend that approval of the resolution be given by this house.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the official opposition approve of this treaty primarily of course because it is to further the safety of life on the great lakes. In the ordinary course we believe it would have been wise to have the agreement considered by one of the committees of the house; but in view of the fact that the session is in its last stages and that the house is sitting such long hours we doubt whether anything would be gained by so doing. The minister did not give that reason for not referring the agreement to a committee; but perhaps if we put his reason and our reason together, we can agree that there should be no reference to a committee. However, since the matter is not to be referred to a committee I should like to place before the minister, on behalf of the official opposition, four or five questions in connection with this agreement, and I hope he will answer them when he closes the debate; or if there is no procedure for him to close the debate, perhaps the house would consent to have him deal with these particular questions.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: USE OF RADIOTELEPHONE ON GREAT LAKES- APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT
speechtext: It is a substantive motion.

subtopic: USE OF RADIOTELEPHONE ON GREAT LAKES- APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT
speechtext:
In the first place, article 3, subsection 2, clause (d) provides that all government vessels are exempt from the provisions of this agreement. That provision will apply not only to Canadian and United States government-owned vessels but also to vessels owned by any foreign government. We believe that these particular vessels should not be exempt. If the vessels are of the size which would call for compliance with the agreement if they are privately owned, then surely government vessels should at least be equipped in the same manner as the private vessels. Perhaps it is the intention that such should be the case. There does not seem to be any reason at all why government vessels should not comply with these provisions which are designed to promote the safety of life. Some vessels coming here
3378	HOUSE OF
Promotion of Safety on Great Lakes which belong to other countries will be owned by foreign governments. Certainly they should have to comply with the provisions.
Then I would point out to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the house that the exemptions contained in this agreement are extremely wide. We hope that the Canadian government will not take advantage of the power to give such wide exemptions. For example in article 3, subsection 2, there is a provision to the effect that where a vessel is not making more than two voyages on the great lakes in any one calendar year, she may be exempted from many of these provisions. It will still be necessary for that vessel to have what is called a safety radiotelephony certificate, and to meet the radio frequency requirements. But as I read this particular part of the agreement such a vessel can be exempted from having an officer or some official on the ship who is qualified, and from carrying out what are the most important requirements contained in the agreement.
In article 6 there are even wider exemptions. If the Department of Transport takes advantage of these powers practically any ship could be exempted. The first subsection of the article reads as follows:
Each contracting government, if it considers that the conditions of the voyage or voyages affecting safety, including but not necessarily limited to the regularity or frequency of the voyages, the route or routes, the maximum distance of the vessel from shore, the length of voyage or voyages, and the absence of general navigation hazards, or other circumstances,-
I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that those specific cases are listed; but there is, in addition, the broad right to exempt to a wider degree. The article continues:
-are such as to render the full application of articles 7, 8, and 9, or any of them, of this agreement unreasonable or unnecessary, may exempt-
And here is the specific power given to the department.
-partially, conditionally, or completely from the provisions of articles 7, 8, and 9, or any of them, any individual vessel for one or more voyages or for any period of time not exceeding one year from the date of exemption.
We hope that little use will be made of those wide exemption powers. If that particular article is used extensively, there is a hole made in the agreement which would render it of comparatively little value. We should like to have from the minister a statement with regard to the policy of the government in granting these exemptions.
Then another question which is bothering us is the provision in article 7 of the agreement for compelling continuous effective listening. Subsection 1, clause (a) provides:
There shall be on board, as an officer or member of the crew of vessel, at least one person whose 

qualifications for radiotelephone operation for safety purposes on the great lakes have been certified by the contracting governments.
That provision, of course, is perfectly reasonable.

subtopic: USE OF RADIOTELEPHONE ON GREAT LAKES- APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT
speechtext: What article is the hon. member reading?

subtopic: USE OF RADIOTELEPHONE ON GREAT LAKES- APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Article 7, subsection 1, clause (a). Then clause (b) of the same subsection reads as follows:
From among those certified persons, the master shall designate one or more who shall operate the radiotelephone installation.
But it goes on to say this:
The duties of the persons so designated need not be restricted to duties in connection with the radiotelephone installation but may include any and all duties assigned them by the master.
In other words, the officer or member of the crew can be a freight checker, a purser, a steward or he can carry on any other duties on the vessel.
Then clause (c) goes even further. It reads:
Except when the radiotelephone installation is being used to transmit or receive on frequencies authorized for the maritime mobile service, there shall be continuous effective listening on the distress frequency by aural means by at least one officer or member of the crew who has been designated by the master to perform such listening.
Then we find this further sentence:
The person so designated by the master may simultaneously perform other duties relating to the operation or navigation of the vessel, provided that such other duties do not interfere with the effectiveness of the listening.
We have had difficulties on the west coast arising out of people having double jobs of that kind. There has been a considerable use of the radiotelephone on vessels, but the person who is supposed to be listening to the radiotelephone may have half a dozen other jobs to do; and even in the case of the radiotelegraph, that is the ordinary Marconi, we have had complaints of Marconi operators being put on other jobs, having to check the freight and look after various other duties, with the result that the radiotelegraph has not been properly watched, and there has been the same trouble with the radiotelephone.
Just a year or so ago we had an instance of a passenger vessel approaching the entrance to Vancouver harbour in a fog. It had a radiotelephone, and the operator on the First Narrows bridge was warning the vessel that it was running into the rocks; and yet, because there was nobody listening, no attention was paid to the warning and the vessel piled up on the rocks of Stanley park.
I should like to warn the minister that making provisions of this kind, whereby the

duties of the man responsible for the radiotelephone can be expanded to cover other different duties, is bound to mean that he pays just that much less attention to the radiotelephone, and the end result is that you greatly weaken your provision for safety of life on the great lakes. I hope that the department will give consideration to that feature when preparing the legislation which is to be submitted next year.
Article 5 provides that:
Each contracting government undertakes to ensure that necessary arrangements are made for a listening watch by coast stations on the distress frequency.
Obviously there is not a great deal of point in compelling ships to have radiotelephone if there are no proper stations on the shore with which they can communicate. We should like to know from the minister whether or not the Department of Transport is now in a position to provide the proper listening watches by coast stations? Will it mean the establishment of more coast stations than there are at the present time, or what is to be done by Canada to implement that particular article of the agreement?
Finally, I can find no provision in this agreement dealing with radiotelegraphy as distinguished from radiotelephony. I would have thought that the agreement would provide that radiotelegraph could be used as an alternative, but there seems to be no such provision. It is hoped that oceangoing vessels will come into the great lakes when the St. Lawrence waterway has been constructed. In all cases these ocean-going vessels will have radio operators. I would think that would be the position with practically all of the ocean-going freighters which would come into the great lakes. I believe that that eventuality should have been foreseen. We would hope that there will not be any removal of the safety provisions in connection with radio on these deep-sea vessels.
As the minister knows, there has been a good deal of complaint in British Columbia about the shipping companies trying to have regulations made so that they could use the radiotelephone instead of using the ordinary Marconi. Some of us who represent coastal ridings have felt that the lives of persons travelling on passenger vessels were being endangered because there were not sufficiently stringent regulations compelling the use of a Marconi operator, and we do not want to have any legislation passed by the Canadian government which would have the effect of making that situation worse even on the great lakes. When the minister closes the debate I would ask him to explain just 55704-214
Promotion of Safety on Great Lakes how the plans for radiotelephony fit in with the ordinary Marconi.
There may be other points which have come to the attention of other opposition parties. We have had this agreement only a short time and there has not been a great deal of opportunity for study. I would ask the minister to deal with these questions which I have raised.

subtopic: USE OF RADIOTELEPHONE ON GREAT LAKES- APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT
speechtext:
The
hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has I think covered the ground pretty well. The questions that he asked of the minister are ones that should be answered. Just as the hon. member says, we have had this agreement so recently in our hands that very little study had been given to it by myself, as a matter of fact, and I have not been back in the house except for the last few days. However, I endorse what he has said regarding the necessity of having competent people on board the lake ships who will be able to take any messages that come to the ship at any time.
Another important matter is that someone among the personnel aboard the ship, whether it be on the lakes, on the Pacific coast or on the Atlantic coast, wherever passengers are carried, should be competent to repair any break-down of the apparatus. I think that is a very important matter. I was on a ship off the Pacific coast a year or two ago, and I found that on most of the ships, while the radar was in operation, there was no one competent to make even a minor repair if anything went wrong with the apparatus. What is true of radar of course is even more true regarding the radiotelephone system. Anything that we can do by way of legislation and regulations to prevent the loss of life at sea, apart altogether from the loss of property involved, we should do in this house. I welcome the agreement. We have had several very serious disasters in the last few years which have given something of a black eye to our shipping on the great lakes as well as in our coastal waters. The more we do in the way of regulation and subsequent legislation to ensure absolute safety-radiotelegraph, Marconi, radar, or whatever it may be -the better it will be for our own shipping interests and for the good name of the country in which we live.
All I wish to say is that we join in supporting the agreement; and we hope that when further amendments are made to the statutes consideration will be given to some of the matters that have arisen and are not covered by this agreement.

subtopic: USE OF RADIOTELEPHONE ON GREAT LAKES- APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to call to the attention
3380	HOUSE OF
Promotion of Safety on Great Lakes of the minister, before this resolution becomes effective, that we have similar problems on the coastal range of the Atlantic. I would mention particularly Northumberland strait. Why could not this provision be made applicable to the Atlantic as well as to the great lakes service?
On several occasions lately I have discussed with the minister the matter of coastguard protection in the Atlantic region. When this resolution is going through, I am wondering why some further protection could not be given to our ships and sailors on the Atlantic seaboard, as well.

subtopic: USE OF RADIOTELEPHONE ON GREAT LAKES- APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know that the type of equipment to which reference is made in this resolution is the same as that used along the Atlantic coast line. I would say however that in my opinion radiotelephone has been of greater assistance to boatmen on the Atlantic coast line than any other improvement in the last fifty years.
When the minister points out that this is an international agreement, I am reminded of the period of time during the war when it was found necessary to discontinue this service. In other words, boats that had been equipped with radiotelephone were obliged to remove that equipment during wartime, and it was of course costly equipment.
In the section from which I come both Canadian and American boats are plying those waters. I would say without fear of successful contradiction that two-thirds of the boats there, even those fifty feet in length, are today equipped with radiotelephones, and it is the greatest convenience one could imagine for those who operate the boats. The radiotelephone service is installed usually by the owners of the freighters and carriers. I would point out however that today many of our individual fishermen have installed a similar service.
Approaching the matter from its international aspect, I would point out that today even taxicabs operating along the international border must disconnect their radiotelephone equipment upon crossing the border, and upon returning it is connected again. This is a great nuisance to those who are operating taxis.
I believe the minister's suggestion is one that will be endorsed by all those who have knowledge of conditions on the water. We know that radiotelephone is a great convenience. I cannot see however that the services of a full-time operator would be necessary. I have said that I am not fully aware that the equipment here indicated is exactly the same as that used along the


Atlantic coast line, but in what I am saying I am taking it for granted that this is so. In those circumstances I think it is not necessary at any time to have a full-time operator. This involves an additional cost for boat owners who are operating under conditions of great expense today, and who must pay high wages.
I support the resolution because I believe any type of radiotelephone connection is helpful in any area where it can be provided.

I am not so sure about the last statement.
I am most grateful to the house for the manner in which the debate has taken place. I have listened with interest to the general approval given to the agreement signed by Canada and the United States, subject of course to certain apparent deficiencies, as they have been pointed out by hon. members who have taken part in the discussion.
The object and purpose of the agreement is of course an excellent one, and this was made particularly evident in the remarks of the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) who made special reference to the beneficial effects of radiotelephone in certain areas.
I believe there can be no doubt that in the minds of a great majority of those using the great lakes, radiotelephone is more efficient than radiotelegraph when operating within a restricted area. That is why I think there must be general agreement as to the purpose and object of this agreement signed between Canada and the United States. Radiotelegraph has of course a greater range, and unquestionably can do a better job on inter-[DOT] national voyages. But within the area covered by this agreement I do not think there is any doubt about the superiority of radiotelephone over radiotelegraph communication. That, at least, seems to be the opinion of the experts.
Turning now to the questions that have arisen, I need not say to the house that when an agreement of this kind has been under

negotiation for several years it must of necessity have been arrived at by compromise. There are many things in the agreement we would have liked to see otherwise; but in our anxiety to reach a decision as to the mandatory installation of telephone equipment on our ships on the great lakes, we did consent to certain compromises.
That is the general answer I would make to some of the objections raised. And, dealing more particularly with those objections, we hear the question asked as to why government vessels are exempt. Our view was that they should not have been exempt. We felt all along that there should have been application of these regulations to our vessels.

subtopic: USE OF RADIOTELEPHONE ON GREAT LAKES- APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT
speechtext: The minister is referring to government vessels?

subtopic: USE OF RADIOTELEPHONE ON GREAT LAKES- APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Yes. However, the other party to the agreement thought otherwise. As a matter of fact I do not think it makes any difference because I can say now that the vast majority if not all of the government vessels operating on the great lakes are today equipped with radiotelephone facilities.
Then there was the suggestion that there are too many exemptions. In article 3 there are exemptions for certain ships, provided they do not make more than two voyages. In article 6 there is a general policy of exemption covering a wider field. It has been asked what the policy of the government is with reference to these additional exemptions. My answer to that is that the Canada Shipping Act, the international convention for the safety of life at sea and this agreement all make provision for certain exemptions. In fact in the Canada Shipping Act there are a number of sections giving the minister discretion, after recommendation from the board of steamship inspection, to grant exemptions. I think there should be exemptions for both parties because I can visualize a number of cases that might well arise when, if it were not possible to grant an exemption, it would be altogether impossible for the ship to go to sea. I can think, for instance, of exemptions now granted under the Canada Shipping Act in cases where the operator of a ship has no qualified mate or an engineer, and consequently would not be able to proceed and his whole operation is held up. There is provision in the act for that kind of exemption.

subtopic: USE OF RADIOTELEPHONE ON GREAT LAKES- APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT
speechtext: The minister is not thinking of the Ming Sung ships, is he?

subtopic: USE OF RADIOTELEPHONE ON GREAT LAKES- APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT
speechtext:
No, I was not thinking of them at this time although I believe that the exemptions in that case were wisely given. They may not have turned out as my hon. friend and I would have wished but I am 55704-2141
Promotion of Safety on Great Lakes still hopeful that notwithstanding the present position it will be possible to recoup a substantial amount of our money involved in those operations. I should like to get back to the exemptions with which I was dealing. It is not the intention of the government to use its discretion widely in granting such exemptions. I should not like to be tied down to what I say now, but I will say that on the contrary our intention is to exempt some ferries and perhaps also in some cases to reduce the power of equipment. Again I should not like to be tied down to this statement, but I will also say that beyond that I cannot visualize any general exercise of the discretionary powers by way of exemption.
I was also asked about the article governing coast station listening watches, how they are operating, is there a sufficient number in operation and will more have to be established. No greater number of listening posts will have to be established than are now in operation. As a matter of fact these listening posts have been in operation since 1938, I believe it is. They are effective and efficient, and we do not think it will be necessary to add to their number. We think that those existing now on the great lakes at places such as Kingston, Toronto, Port Burwell, Point Edward, Midland, Sault Ste. Marie and Port Arthur are sufficient to look after the operation of shipping on the great lakes at least on our side of the boundary line.
I was asked to differentiate between radiotelephone and radiotelegraph operations and to say why there is no provision here for radiotelegraph. I think I anticipated the answer in my opening remarks when I said that radiotelephone is more effective in a shorter range. The reason why radiotelegraph is excluded entirely from the operation of this agreement is that the range of radiotelephone is all that is required for the protection of life and property within the area of the great lakes. The law as it now stands is found in section 406 (2) (a) of the Canada Shipping Act which provides for the installation of radiotelegraph equipment on certain vessels. For instance the act requires passenger steamships to carry radiotelegraph apparatus and a radio operator when they fall within one of the three following categories, namely, (1) carrying fifty or more persons and going on a voyage of more than 200 nautical miles; (2) carrying 250 or more persons: and going on a voyage of more than 90 nautical miles; and (3) carrying 500 or more persons and going on a voyage of more than 20 nautical miles.
In addition, there is provision in section 406 (2) (b) covering the requirements for cargo vessels of 5,000 gross tons and over. They have to carry radiotelegraph apparatus and a radio operator on voyages of more than 200
3382	HOUSE OF
Promotion of Safety on Great Lakes nautical miles. The law as it exists now is covered in those two sections. Then of course there is the international convention for the safety of life at sea which excludes the great lakes.

subtopic: USE OF RADIOTELEPHONE ON GREAT LAKES- APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT
speechtext: Includes or excludes?

subtopic: USE OF RADIOTELEPHONE ON GREAT LAKES- APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Excludes the great lakes. Therefore this agreement with reference to the compulsory installation of radiotelephone equipment will be restricted to the area of the great lakes as far east as the lower exit of the Lachine canal. Any ships travelling beyond the great lakes into the gulf of St. Lawrence and from there into the ocean, or vice versa, will be subject not only to this agreement but also to the international convention for the safety of life at sea which requires the installation of radiotelegraph equipment. That is the distinction which exists between the radiotelegraph and the radiotelephone and the reason why radiotelegraph is not included in the agreement.
Some objection was raised on the ground that it is not a good thing to allow an operator to do more than one job. It was said that it was not a good thing to have a man carry on as a boatswain, a mate or an assistant mate and at the same time listen to the telephone. I think the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) covered that. I do not know if my hon. friend has been on these ships when they are in operation. I have on a number of occasions, and I think the procedure is simple and one which works out quite satisfactorily. The loudspeaker is on the bridge and is tuned in to the frequency of 2182 kilocycles. There are always two if not more persons on the bridge, the master and a couple of mates. With that frequency tuned in it is a very simple thing for a man to listen to the radiotelephone and at the same time carry on his duties as mate, assistant mate or second assistant mate.
I have seen it done frequently in the summer months and I think it operates efficiently. There is no doubt but that the two parties to this agreement thought so, and I am sure they came to that conclusion because of the experience their nationals have had over the years. Some question was raised whether this agreement is applicable to the Atlantic region. The treaty covers the great lakes and the operation of ships between Canada and the United States. It is not made applicable to the Atlantic region. What is applicable to the Atlantic region is sections 406 (2) (a) and 406 (2) (b) of the Canada Shipping Act which require the installation of radiotelegraph equipment and the operation of that equipment. A good many ships now operating in that area have radiotelephone.


It is not mandatory but they have it over and above the radiotelegraph equipment. That position will be covered by an amendment to section 406 of the act which it is proposed to bring in at the next session of parliament when we implement this agreement.

speechtext: Might I ask the minister a question? When you speak of radiotelegraph and radiotelephone, would it not be necessary with radiotelegraph to have trained and experienced operators, whereas with radiotelephone any officer of the ship could operate?

speechtext: Yes, my hon. friend is quite right in that assumption. I do not know that I can add much more to this because, as I indicated earlier, there will be full opportunity to discuss the terms of this agreement when the amendment to section 406 of the Canada Shipping Act is brought in at the next session of parliament. I here state that I will introduce that amendment and I take it that in the usual course it will be referred to the appropriate committee.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee took recess I was just about to make some comments on this bill to revise the capital structure of the Canadian National Railway Company. This matter was debated at some length in the house. The bill has also been before the special committee, and there is no need for me to occupy much time. However, I should like to say a few things partly for the sake of getting them on the record, and there are one or two quotations I wish to give from the proceedings of the committee.
First of all I want to remind this committee, as has been said before, of the fact that this is a problem which has been before us for many years and the reasons for which we know. Shortly after the first great war it became necessary to amalgamate into one railway system several lines which had been privately owned and several lines which had been publicly owned, and which had the one common feature that they were all in difficulties. The railway was put together first of all in a rather haphazard manner, perhaps the best that could be done in the circumstances, and in the early 1920's just after this had been done there was a period of great doubt, anxiety and scepticism in the public mind whether the situation could continue or whether we might have to amalgamate all our railways into one unit. Most of us in the house are very glad that was not done because we dislike monopolies, even that strange creation called a democratic monopoly which is so dear to some members of the house, and which I always find it difficult to understand.
At any rate, that situation continued until the 1930's, which of course was a period of fresh difficulty. At that time the Duff commission was appointed and I should like to read a short extract from the report of that very able commission for the purpose of putting it on the record and also because it endorses the necessity of what is being done in this measure besides containing
[Mr. Pouliot.l

a warning which I think it is useful for us to remember. At page 30 of the report of the Duff commission I find the following:
. . . this commission is of opinion that it must be frankly recognized that a very substantial part of the money invested in the railways comprised within the Canadian National system must be regarded as lost and that its capital liabilities should be heavily written down . . .
That was the statement made by the Duff commission, but they did not regard that period of great economic distress as a desirable time to readjust the capital structure. I also wish to refer to another passage in the report of the Duff commission where they say that reasonable protection should be given to the privately-owned undertaking against arbitrary action by the publicly-owned undertaking which might unfairly prejudice the interests of the privately-owned undertaking.
On that score I should merely like to comment that when the two railways appeared before the Turgeon commission there was welcome evidence of good feeling and understanding along with healthy rivalry and competition and sympathy for each other's difficulties and problems. Mainly as a result of the report of the Duff commission we have the two railways and we have this healthy competition which has been greatly to our advantage and has provided us with two railway systems which I think can be regarded as admirable.
I should also like to refer to the measure of relief that was given in 1937 when the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, then minister of transport, recommended to the house that a very large measure of relief be given, something over $1 billion, and that was in fact done. Finally we have the report of the Turgeon commission which recommended various further easements. I I was going to say that they are comprehended in this bill but it would be more accurate to say that the government's decision, based on the Turgeon report, as to v/hat it recommends to the house is in this bill.
The bill has been before the committee. There is little need of my talking at length about it. As I shall indicate in a moment, the bill is believed to carry out the immediate objective. The disappointing thing about it, perhaps inevitably disappointing, is that I did not feel-I do not think anyone will disagree with this statement-that the railway or the department was able to tell us they felt sure that they had found a principle of action which enabled them to assure us that this second major operation on the finances of the railway would be the final operation. However, they felt that it was beneficial and

that it could be brought forward and recommended to the house. I think it is of interest to read briefly what the president of the railway, Mr. Gordon, said about it. I am referring to the evidence Mr. Gordon gave before the committee.

When we made our submission to the royal commission, as I said in my statement, I based it on the opinion, after analysis, that we needed relief, that is, that the Canadian National needed relief in the form of fixed interest charges of roughly $30 million a year. What I am saying about this bill is that it means that the actual relief that we get by the transfer of this $736 million into 4 per cent preferred stock would relieve us of fixed interest charges, plus the adjustments that we get in connection with the $100 million on behalf of Newfoundland, plus this arrangement in section 6, to give us an amount of equity capital each year, plus the prairie adjustment; so that when you put all of those together, you get the effect which in essence is the equivalent of $30 million a year relief. It is not exactly the same in form, but it is the same in quantum of relief, and it is in a better form in our opinion.
I read that because I think it is of importance to know whether the man who is primarily responsible for the operation of the railway did in fact feel that the measure before us would give the relief which is necessary.
As I indicated, there are some things which are disappointing. It would have been more satisfactory if we had been able to discern a principle in the amount of relief that was given, but I think the only principle you can find is that those responsible felt that a certain relief was needed and they took the means by one device and another to make up to the total amount of relief desired.
The other comments I wish to make can come up as we reach the appropriate sections of the bill, with the exception of one point. There is one comment I wish to make on a matter that seems to me to be of some importance. It arose before the committee and I hope it is relevant and proper to raise it here. I refer to the directors of the Canadian National Railways.
The directors of the Canadian National Railways are outstanding citizens, and nothing I say is intended to reflect or criticize them in the slightest possible degree. However, this I will say. I feel that with advantage to the railway the board might be enlarged. That suggestion is put by some on
Canadian National Railways a geographical basis, that we should have all parts of the country represented from a geographical point of view. Personally I am not so concerned with that. I think it is more desirable to have a good man from British Columbia than a bad man from Ontario; but I feel ever so strongly that in the tremendous task which has been assigned to Mr. Gordon, for whom I have the highest respect, he needs the assistance of all the ability he can get. Do not misunderstand me, I do not believe myself that directors run a railway company. I know they do not and they should not. Nevertheless, if you look at the Canadian Pacific Railway you will find they have a large board. Secondly, you will find an extraordinary percentage of men holding key business positions. The advantage is that those men, even though they may meet very seldom, and even though they do not try to interfere with management-which they should not do

make available their advice. It is the advice of a large group of the ablest businessmen in the country. I am very confident that if Mr. Gordon were standing here now, and he were asked whether he would like to have the best information from the widest variety of sources, he would agree.
Let me say again that nothing I have said is intended to cast the slightest criticism on the members of the board. I have the highest regard for those whom I know. My suggestion is that the board might be added to, giving new resources of experience and knowledge, imagination and all the things needed to assist in running this enterprise. I suppose it is by far the greatest enterprise we have in Canada, and I make my suggestion in the hope that the minister may find it possible to consider it. It is not original anf it was made at the time of the committee sittings, but I make it again in order that it may be on the record.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks at this stage of the bill will be very brief. We have already had a discussion on the principle of this amending legislation in the earlier stages, and we shall be able to deal with the details when we get into committee. Also we have made it clear that we support this legislation so far as it goes. However, I should like to make it clear once again that from a study of the principles underlying the funding of insurance of this kind and from a study of the amounts that are on hand in the unemployment insurance fund we feel that there is too great a disparity between the premium payments required of those insured and the benefits paid. In our view either one thing or the other should be done. Either the amount of benefits paid under the act should be increased or the premium payments required of those insured should be decreased. Our preference is for the former, that the amount of the benefits should be increased, having regard to the suggestions made to the government by the major labour congresses in this country.
As we have indicated on previous occasions, another shortcoming in the Unemployment Insurance Act, and I regret that there seems to be nothing in the amending legislation now before us to take care of it, has to do with the position of the unemployment insurance benefit recipients who, while on those benefits, become ill. I realize that the minister made a statement the other day on this point. I hope he has given thought to the reply I made to his statement, and that further consideration will yet be given that phase of the matter. This is entirely apart from the question of any sickness benefits that might be obtained under a health insurance program. Entirely apart from that, we believe that when a person is drawing unemployment insurance benefits, having qualified in every way for these benefits, he should not be cut off from them because he takes ill; particularly when, as in many instances is the situation, there is still no work for him.
There are two or three other matters in which we are interested but which we can deal with when we get into committee. I referred to some of these matters in the earlier stages. At the moment I shall leave


it at that, expressing our very strong views with respect to those two matters which we feel to be very important.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE RATES OF BENEFIT, TO REDUCE THE NUMBER OF WAITING DAYS BEFORE RECEIPT OF BENEFIT, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to say a word at this time also. When the minister's estimates were before the house I made quite a lengthy statement in regard to section 38, regulation 5 (a), having to do with married women. Perhaps the minister and his advisers have read the Hansard report of that speech. I feel very strongly on that point, because there is rank discrimination in so far as married women are concerned when they lose their employment. I am just wondering whether the minister has any intention of making some amendments to regulation 5 (a) when the bill is in committee, because as it reads at the present time it practically deals out a married woman, despite the fact that she is supposed to be insured during the period of her employment.
I mention that now so the minister can give us some indication as to whether or not there is any intention of proposing an amendment to the regulation. It would not require much of an amendment to accomplish the purpose. Certainly it is inflexible at the present time.
I should like to say a word or two in support of the contention of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that while a person is sick these payments should not be discontinued. I stressed this matter a couple of years ago in the house, but apparently there has not been much change in that regard. The position is that in many industries across Canada employees pay into a sick benefit fund. This is a form of insurance against being without funds when they are ill. As it is a form of insurance, they are legitimately entitled to receive that sick benefit for the period during which they are ill. Since that time the Unemployment Insurance Act has been passed.
There will be many men, particularly those employed in the heavy industries such as the steel plants, the coal mines and the automobile factories, places where the work is very heavy, who will find themselves ill and will not be able to carry on their normal work. These men may not be bedridden, but they receive the benefits of their insurance plan for which they have already paid, and from which they are entitled legitimately to collect.
At the same time they are not employed in their regular occupations and they have another form of insurance for which they are paying, covering the period of their unemployment. The person who is in the dual position of being insured on two counts,

upon making application for his sick benefit is ruled immediately as ineligible for unemployment insurance. If he does not make application for his sick benefit and is registered as being unemployed, he places himself in the position of serving notice on his employer severing his employment.
In industry there are pension plans based upon the amount of time a man has worked. While a worker may be ill for only three weeks or a month, he must forgo his sick benefits if he wishes to receive unemployment insurance. If he takes the unemployment insurance, he thus severs his employment with his employer and may not get back on the payroll again.
This is a question which I suggest the unemployment insurance authorities should discuss with industrialists. I refer to the situation where there is a sick benefit plan in operation. These sick benefit plans came into being many years before the Unemployment Insurance Act was passed, and have carried on since that time.
I suggest that the man who is incapacitated for a short period of time, and may not be able to carry on his regular form of heavy employment, has a legitimate claim on both counts to the insurance for which he has paid. There should be an understanding on the part of the commission that a man who has registered as unemployed for a month or so should not be faced with an employer who takes the adamant attitude that the employee must be struck off the payroll, and will not be permitted to return to work. If the insurance is to be paid both ways, then there should be some co-ordination in administration. There should be some understanding.
I am not blaming the commission, because it has been my experience that in so far as it is within their power they are willing to co-operate. The adamant attitude is the one taken by the employer, and I am now referring particularly to the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation in Nova Scotia. This matter has been discussed time and again in union circles, and I am just wondering if the minister and some of his officials might take a look into it and have a talk with the employer in this particular instance, because in my opinion he is the one who is taking the unreasonable attitude. It is up to someone to prove to the employer that this attitude is not reasonable.
I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) brought up an important point. I receive a good deal of correspondence from people who say, "We have paid unemployment insurance for five years, or since the inception of the plan. We are
Unemployment Insurance Act laid off when sick, and stay away for a few months, during which time we have no income. When we apply for unemployment insurance we are told we cannot get it because we did not sever our employment in the way set out in the act. We are told that ill health or sickness is not a justification for drawing unemployment insurance." Nevertheless these persons are not working, and have no income. Some of them suggest they should have a return of the premiums they have paid in, and that has been the general point of view discussed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. On the other hand the problem of dual insurance is one that should be discussed with employers with a view to arriving at some measure of co-ordination and understanding, so the insurance payments will be made for the purposes for which the two kinds of insurance were established.
I do not expect the minister to reply now, but I do expect him to take the matter under advisement and, at some time in the future, to give an explanation of what might be done, after he has consulted with employers and the others concerned.

I should like to press for some action with regard to this regulation. Speaking in the house the other night at the resolution stage I made some remarks with reference to the reduction of the period from 90 days. At that time I said I could see that there might


be difficulties in establishing intention, but that no fault could be found with reducing the period in the first instance to 60 days.
However, I must admit that since that time, having considered the matter further at some length, I have come to the conclusion that I was very lenient in that regard. I can see no reason why this section should not be taken right out of the regulations. I know the arguments that are put forward by the department. I know the difficulties with which the local offices are faced; but in my opinion they are no more difficult than those with which they are faced with respect to numerous employees in many lines of activity. To say that misrepresentation or malingering is confined only to one section of the labour force is in my opinion a reflection on the integrity of that particular group of citizens. I can see no reason at all why this regulation was put in the act in the first place. It has only been in effect for about two years, and has been operative for only a little more than a year. I can see no reason why this particular group was singled out for discrimination. It is not only a reflection on the integrity of working women but in my opinion it is also an intrusion on their civil rights.
Consideration of the matter from this angle has caused me to speak today in stronger terms than those in which I spoke the other evening at the resolution stage of the bill. While I was willing at that time to see the regulations relaxed somewhat, I now say I believe firmly that this particular provision should be stricken from the regulations as they now stand. I ask the minister to give this matter very careful consideration. I am sure there are other ways of handling this problem, and that it is no more serious among this class of workers than among all the other classes with which the commission deals. This section and the difficulty which is encountered with respect thereto lead me also to urge the contention I made the other night that there should be a woman member of the commission. As I said at that time, it is of course impossible to have such representation under the present set-up of the commission unless its membership is enlarged.
In the tenth annual report of the unemployment insurance commission there is a table on page 44 which deals with placements in regular and casual employment. I was interested to note that so far as regular placements are concerned those of women represent 36.3 per cent or well over one-third of those of men. As to casual placements the proportion is much higher. Casual placements of women were 63 per cent of those of men. Totalling the two and

figuring out the average, female placements represented 40 per cent of male placements. I feel that in itself supports the contention that if the working forces of the Dominion of Canada contain within their numbers such a large percentage of women, then women should be represented on the commission by someone who understands those problems which are not so easily argued by fact and logic.
On page 28 of the same report there is a table of placements of handicapped people during 1950. Here again the number of female placements is well over one-third of male placements. That appears to be the case pretty well throughout the picture. On page 25 of the report special mention is made of the increased number of women in the labour market in Canada. I should like to read into the record a paragraph which deals with this problem. It is headed, "Increase of women in labour market", and reads as follows:
During 1950 there was a steady increase in the number of female applicants registered at local offices of the commission for whom it was not possible to find suitable employment. It is believed that the increase was due, in part at least, to the rising cost of living in Canada and the necessity for married women to seek employment in order to augment the family income. However, notwithstanding a steady demand from employers for stenographers and typists, many women registered in these occupations could not be referred to employers because they were married and no longer in the lower age brackets.
I recognize, Mr. Chairman, that this is a problem which has many sides, but whatever the reason may be for the increased entry into employment of women of all ages and all amounts of experience, we must nevertheless recognize now that it is a condition of modern living. Inasmuch as it is a condition of modern living we can no longer close our eyes to it. We must accept it. For this reason I am more than ever convinced that the efficiency of the commission would be enhanced by its enlargement to include a woman member thereof. This belief is confirmed by a booklet, "Unemployment Insurance in Canada, 1940-1950," issued by the industrial relations section of the university of Montreal. After describing in a general way the workings of unemployment insurance in Canada in the ten-year period it winds up with this paragraph:
If the unemployment insurance commission in its administrative task continues to give priority to the human problems of the individual, if day after day it betters its relations with the insured, if it encourages its personnel to pursue intellectual and moral culture, the commission will thus give to the law a more human and more socially valuable function.
I think that is perfectly true, Mr. Chairman, and I think it is a plea which might well be heeded by this house. In order to

When speaking at the resolution stage of this bill, I brought to the minister's attention the particular case of a man in my riding who had contributed to the unemployment insurance scheme ever since its inception eleven years ago. He had built up a credit of more than $900, and last November became unemployed. He drew benefits for thirteen days, and then had to enter hospital for an eye operation. As soon as he entered hospital his unemployment insurance benefits were cut off. After the man had been released from the hospital, being totally blind, I was notified. I brought the matter to the attention of the house through a letter written to me regarding my inquiry about that man, explaining why these unemployment insurance benefits had been cut off.
This letter had been written by Mr. B. G. Sullivan, Ontario regional supervisor, saying how much the commission regretted the action but at that time the man did not come under the regulations and could no longer, therefore, be paid unemployment insurance benefits. I also drew to the minister's attention the fact that I insisted on the Canadian National Institute for the Blind being notified. On my insistence they were notified and guards were provided so the man could resume his employment. I pointed out to the minister that, unfortunately, none of this would have taken place if I had not brought the matter to the attention of the unemployment insurance commission and requested, very strongly I may add, that they notify the Canadian National Institute for the Blind.

In view of that incident, I should like to know what instructions the minister has sent out to the employees of the unemployment insurance commission concerning the steps they should take when a man or woman who has built up an unemployment insurance credit is prevented from working because of a permanent disability. What does the minister suggest they should do in order to see that a disabled man or woman is enabled to continue work, by means of guards or aids, as in the case of the man I mentioned?
The second point I should like the minister to answer is this. As I pointed out in speaking earlier, the unemployment insurance credits which a man or woman builds up are built up through contributions made by that man or woman and his or her employer.

But mostly by contributions made by the man or woman and the employer. I believe those credits belong to that man or woman by right. They exist because the man or woman built them up so they would be available if for any reason the man or woman became unemployed. When a permanent disability takes place the unemployment insurance commission completely cuts that man or woman off from unemployment insurance benefits, as in the case of the man I mentioned. The man in the case I cited had a credit of over $900, and the commission was quite willing to cut him off from that credit for all time by simply stating, in so many words, "That money no longer belongs to you; you have no right to it because you are permanently disabled."
I believe that is completely wrong. There is no time when a man or woman needs unemployment insurance credits nearly as badly as when he or she becomes totally disabled and thereby prevented from earning a living. Not only do they have to go on providing for themselves and their families, but in most cases they have doctor and hospital bills to pay as well. I believe there are many more reasons why those unemployment insurance credits should be paid to those people than to people who are just temporarily unemployed.
I feel sure that in answering the minister will tell me the Unemployment Insurance Act has been set up on an actuarially sound basis which does not take into consideration payments to people in the totally disabled category. However, I believe that if the commission's doctors have examined a man or woman and certified that he or she is permanently disabled and cannot earn a living, then the unemployment insurance commission should pay those people the credits standing in their name.

Unemployment Insurance Act
In addition to emphasizing that view I should like to point out that when the act was amended in 1950 it was worded in such a way with respect to section 31 of the act, which we are now considering under clause 4 of this bill, as to create quite a bit of confusion in the minds of many workers as to the benefits to which they were entitled on becoming unemployed. Some of us pointed out when this was being put through in 1950 that there was more than confusion involved; that there was actually a certain loss of an alleged increase. The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Labour will probably recall that he and I had quite a debate over the effect of the wording in section 31 (2) (b) as it stands at the present time in the main act. That clause reads:
In computing the average daily contribution (a) one cent shall be deducted from each daily contribution paid by the insured person after the first day of July, nineteen hundred and fifty.
I pointed out to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Labour and to the Minister of National Health and Welfare who was piloting the bill on that occasion that the result of that clause being in there where we are told how a worker computes his benefit, is that when the worker looks at the table to ascertain his benefit he must move one line above the amount he is paying in to ascertain the amount of benefit he will draw out. I need not rehash the argument we had on that occasion. My position has certainly been vindicated, at least in my own experience, by the large number of letters I have had on this very point. Many a time I have had to explain to an unemployed worker why he was receiving not the benefit set directly opposite the amount he had been paying in, but rather the amount directly opposite and up one line. The reason for that is the section which I have just read from the main act.
I want to repeat my opposition to the substance of what was done on that occasion and to the confusion that it created. I am glad to note that, at least the confusion is being resolved in the amending section now before us. But all that is resolved is the confusion; it does not make any change in substance. The terms of clause 4, which are now before us, when we get over to the table that is included in that clause, are different from the table at present in the act. That difference of course can be seen by looking at the table in its former state as it appears on the right hand page of the bill that is now before us. For example, the table on the opposite side formerly had opposite 3 cents the sum of $1 per day for a person without dependents. That was not really the case, for the qualifying clause which I read meant that a person had to move up one line. Thus his daily

Unemployment Insurance Act benefit was only 70 cents. In the new version of this table it is made clear that the person whose contribution is 3 cents draws only 70 cents a day. As I say, Mr. Chairman, I am glad to see that the confusion has been resolved and that from here on workers, when they look at that table, will not wonder why they draw a benefit less than what would seem to be that to which they are entitled. I am sorry that is as far as this correction goes.

Clause 12 amends section 83 of the act, which is one of the sections under the general heading "unemployment insurance advisory committee". In fact this is the section which spells out the constitution of that committee and certain of its powers and functions. While we are on this clause I should like to take a moment to express to the minister my very strong views with regard to any change that may be made in the functioning of the advisory committees at the three levels. The minister knows that what I have in mind is covered by the difference between circular letter No. 18 and a proposed circular letter No. 19. As I understand it, under the present arrangement the avenue of travel between these committees is vertical. The local committees make their reports and recommendations to the regional committees and the regional committees in turn to the national advisory committee. In return the replies to those reports and recommendations, and any suggestions, travel the other way. That is provided for in circular letter No. 18, which spells out the way in which the committees are to function. As the minister knows-and this is set out in the section with which we are now dealing -these are people who are outside the direct employment of the unemployment insurance commission, and who represent labour and management. They are there to give advice.
It appears that there is some thought of changing the way those committees function

and suggesting that the local committees should have their contact and their way of reporting only through the local civil service side of the unemployment insurance commission; and that similarly the regional advisory committees should maintain their liaison with the regional officials through the civil service side of the unemployment insurance commission.
It has been represented to me by some of those who are interested in the matter that the present set-up has some very desirable features that should not be lost. Those who take this view fear that if there is a change to the other pattern, many good ideas born or hatched at the local level will never get to the point where they may really be considered.
Without in any way reflecting upon the efficiency with which the officials of the commission carry out their duties, there is a tendency on the part of officials to be concerned only in keeping things going as they are. So long as things are running along all right, so long as "Everything's up to date in my department"-and in this I am borrowing from a song we heard not long ago at the press gallery dinner-there is nothing to worry about.
I share the views of those who expressed the thought to me that the ideas generated in the local committees would not get very far past the local officials if that change were made. When I sought to have tabled a copy of circular letter No. 19 the minister informed me that it was only a proposed circular letter, and that it had not yet been put in final form. He pointed out that therefore it could not be tabled. Naturally I have no objection to there being a circular letter No. 19, or to there being a review of the pattern set out in circular letter No. 18; but I would hope that the proposed circular letter No. 19 might be reviewed before it is put in final form.
If any changes are felt desirable, let it not be at the expense of the loss of values to be obtained from getting ideas from the local level right up to the top level and back again, and securing the views and the opinions of advisory committees at all levels. It is not necessary to spend more time on the subject now, but I do urge the minister to give consideration to the point of view I am putting forward today, and which I understand has been expressed by some of the local and regional advisory committees.

Previously the calculation of the average daily contribution, which is the basis of regular benefit, included the deduction of one cent collected for the purpose of the supplementary benefit. IMr. Cote (Verdun-La Salle).]
The section if amended would read:
This act shall be administered by a commission to be called "The Unemployment Insurance Commission," which shall consist of four commissioners, who shall be appointed by the governor in council, one of whom shall be a chief commissioner and one of whom shall be a woman.
My predecessor in the chair earlier in the day, the deputy chairman, suggested to the hon. member for Hamilton West that this addition of a section to the bill might more properly be considered after consideration of section 20, since it is an addition to the bill. Citation 670, as it appears in Beauchesne's third edition, page 232, confirms that view. It says:
In committee all the clauses of the bill are considered before any new clauses are brought up and added to the bill. But this practice is not rigorously followed and the committee is generally guided by what is most convenient in each particular case.
I think he was quite right in considering that it was more convenient to discuss this after dealing with section 20 since it is an addition to the bill.
A point of order has been raised by the Minister of Labour, that the amendment would not be in order because it would give the government a direct order to expend some additional money. It would increase the financial responsibility of the government. I have looked at the act and find that the addition of one member would make an additional expenditure of $9,000 a year since that is the present salary of each of the commissioners who are now appointed. Therefore it is a case upon which decisions have been rendered on many occasions in the past. Perhaps I might refer hon. members to citation 453 which appears in Beauchesne's third edition at page 171 and which reads as follows:
The tendency has been in the Canadian House of Commons, for the past twenty-five years, to rule out all motions purporting to give the government a direct order to do a thing which cannot be done without the expenditure of money.
Citation 437 of Beauchesne's third edition, page 167, reads in part:
No principle is better understood than the constitutional obligation that rests upon the executive government, of alone initiating measures imposing charges upon the public exchequer.
From time to time rulings based on these citations have been appealed. I have one in mind which appears at page 306 of the Journals for Tuesday, 29th November, 1949, when Bill No. 194 was under consideration in the committee of the whole. The hon. member for Assiniboia moved at that time that clause 4, subclause 2 be amended by deleting therefrom the words "fifty per centum'' and by substituting therefor the words "seventy-five per centum". The chairman ruled the amendment out of order on

the ground that it increased the financial responsibility of the government. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre appealed from the ruling of the chairman, and that ruling was sustained.
Basing my ruling on the citations I have just quoted, I am sorry but I must declare the amendment out of order.
