speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Resources and Development) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REVISE AND CONSOLIDATE, ETC.
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 337, respecting the Northwest Territories.
He said: Hon. members will recall that at the second last session of parliament a number of amendments were made to the Northwest Territories Act. Recognizing the continued and healthy growth of the territories, the principal amendment provided to the citizens of the territories the opportunity to elect three out of the total of eight members of the territorial council. The election was held under the supervision of the chief electoral officer, and the three newly elected members joined with their five appointed colleagues at the first meeting of the council ever to be held in the territories. It assembled in Yellowknife on December 10, 1951, and its opening was attended by proper ceremonial. The citizens of Yellowknife, through the warmth of their reception, their interest and enthusiasm, showed clearly that they welcomed this evidence of their new status.
The Northwest Territories Act was first passed in 1869. There have been several revisions and consolidations since then. The last revision was in 1927. The present Northwest Territories Act is contained in chapter 142 of the Revised Statutes of 1927, and four amending acts were passed in 1938, 1940, 1948 and 1951. The legislative powers conferred upon the commissioner in council by the present act are set out in sections 9 and 10, which confer upon the commissioner in council legislative jurisdiction over most of the subjects in which, under the British North America Act, the various provinces of Canada have jurisdiction.
There are several other matters in respect of which provinces usually have jurisdiction

Northwest Territories Act and in respect of which it is now proposed to confer jurisdiction upon the commissioner in council of the territories. These are roads, wills, the property of married women, coroners and inquests, controverted elections, the manufacture and possession of intoxicants, the establishment, maintenance and management of hospitals, and agriculture. At the present time all these matters are within the jurisdiction only of parliament. However, with the rapid progress in economic development in the territories and the substantial increase in population consequent thereto, it is now considered desirable to authorize the legislature of the territories to deal with these matters, and to repeal sections of the Northwest Territories Act dealing specifically with them.
In the past there has not been, nor is there now, statutory provision for the establishment of a consolidated revenue fund into which territorial revenues from direct taxation within the territories are paid and out of which disbursements for territorial purposes may be made. It is therefore proposed that there be in the Northwest Territories Act a provision for a territorial revenue account which will be maintained as a separate account in the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.
The territorial court was disestablished in 1905, when the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta were created out of the territories. Since that time judicial functions, both civil and criminal, have been exercised by stipendiary magistrates, who have the powers, authorities and functions which were vested in a judge of the supreme court of the Northwest Territories prior to its disestablishment. The increase in population in recent years has resulted in an increase in the number of civil and criminal cases requiring trial by an experienced judge. It is therefore now considered desirable to re-establish the territorial court. It is proposed that the judge of the territorial court of the Yukon Territory will be ex officio the judge of the territorial court of the Northwest Territories, thus providing for the proper trial of cases without the necessity of appointing an additional judge. Corollary thereto, it is proposed also to provide for the appointment of police magistrates, in whom will be vested power to try minor civil and criminal cases, and who will have jurisdiction comparable to that exercised by police magistrates in the provinces. The present stipendiary magistrates resident in the territories will be appointed police magistrates.
Consequent upon the re-establishment of the territorial court, it is also proposed to
IMr. Winters.]
redefine the areas in respect of which provincial courts have concurrent jurisdiction with territorial courts. At the present time the superior courts of the provinces of Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island have in all parts of the territories east of the 89th meridian, and the superior courts of the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia have in all parts of the territories west of the 89th meridian, the same jurisdiction in civil matters arising in the territories as they have in respect of matters arising within the territorial limits of their ordinary jurisdiction. This has in some cases led to abuse. For example, writs have been issued in Edmonton against residents of Aklavik, with the result that the defendants have been put to extraordinary expense in making their defence at a place so far from their normal place of residence. Aklavik, located on the Arctic ocean, is 1,300 miles from Edmonton and there are no highways or railways leading to it.
It is of course still desirable to provide concurrent jurisdiction for areas of the territories where the population is sparse. It is therefore proposed to limit concurrent jurisdiction to the superior courts of the provinces of Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland in civil matters respecting persons and property in the territories east of the 102nd meridian, and to repeal the present provision for concurrent jurisdiction ini respect of matters arising west of the 102nd meridian.
Provision is made for appeals to the court of appeal of Alberta from judgments respecting matters in areas west of the 102nd meridian, and to the courts of appeal of the provinces exercising concurrent jurisdiction in matters arising east of the 102nd meridian. It might be helpful if I stated that the 89th meridian passes through Hudson bay and the 102nd meridian is the boundary between Manitoba and Saskatchewan.
This bill seeks authority to have jurisdiction conferred upon the commissioner in council with regard to the manufacture and possession of intoxicants. At the present time this jurisdiction is vested in parliament although the commissioner in council now has jurisdiction regarding the sale of liquor. This double jurisdiction has caused some confusion, and it is considered desirable to delete from the Northwest Territories Act provisions regarding the manufacture and possession of intoxicants, so that all legislation relating to the manufacture, possession and sale of intoxicants may be contained in one statute, namely the territorial liquor ordinance.

It is proposed to delete from the act a number of sections relating to criminal matters. These will now be contained in the revised Criminal Code.
Another section of the bill would confer upon the governor in council authority to make regulations concerning reindeer. As hon. members may be aware, since 1933 the government of Canada has maintained reindeer herds in the territories for the benefit of natives. There are now three herds managed by native herders. It is planned to establish at least two more during the next few years and it is therefore considered desirable to give to the governor in council authority to make regulations concerning such reindeer.
There are several other minor amendments which I do not think need be mentioned at this time.
The bill contains 48 sections. Of these only 23 either are new or embody substantial changes from the present act. The remaining 25 sections are included chiefly to effect a consolidation and embody no substantial changes in the provisions of the present act.
The present act with amendments to date contains 117 sections. Seventy-two sections have been dropped. As mentioned, these sections refer to criminal law, coroners and juries, married women's property, wills and other miscellaneous subjects, all of vJhich are adequately covered in other legislation or will be covered by territorial ordinance.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REVISE AND CONSOLIDATE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this bill can be welcomed by the house in that it is merely bringing up to date what is in fact the constitution of the Northwest Territories. I would hope to see in the near future the ratio of the elected members to appointed members of the council increased in favour of the elected members. However, as the area of the territory is so vast one cannot as yet treat the area in the same way a province is treated; and possibly one will not be able to do so for many years to come.
The other hope one can have is for the establishment of a superior court in the territory. I realize that this also is a matter of difficulty. In the past litigants have suffered tremendous hardships in travelling to the superior courts of the various provinces. The distances even in the territories are greater than that across the Atlantic ocean. That illustration will give the house some idea, perhaps, of the tremendous size of the territory involved.
In passing I should like merely to mention the job that was done in driving the reindeer herd. There have been a number of scientists and other men such as explorers who have done a job which I think is unique in all
Northwest Territories Act the history of treks. For seven years the reindeer on which the economy of the Eskimo so largely depends were driven from their original feeding grounds into the eastern Arctic. The epic of the drive of those reindeer herds is, in my opinion, one of the great sagas in the history of the north.
I welcome this bill. If there are any objections to it, I feel they can be dealt with as we go through the bill clause by clause.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REVISE AND CONSOLIDATE, ETC.
speechtext: I notice that this section refers to roads, streets, lanes and trails. What is proposed with respect to the construction of roads and streets in this enormous area? Are there to be special appropriations in the estimates to provide for streets in small communities? Who will be responsible for the expenditure of those moneys? What engineers are there in the area, including the built-up communities? Have those areas been surveyed, with due regard to their natural resources, mineral developments and the like?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REVISE AND CONSOLIDATE, ETC.
speechtext:
All the communities have been surveyed and laid out. Some of them are a good size, the largest being Yellowknife, Fort Smith and Hay River. The system of providing roads is one which has grown up over the years. In most cases each project was treated on its merits. Today this has been somewhat regularized, so that the roads have been divided into three general classifications.
The first of these is resource roads. These are roads intended to enable the resources of the area to flow into the economy of Canada, and they are considered to be the responsibility of the federal government. They are built and maintained out of funds appropriated by parliament.
The second classification is that of trunk roads. These are roads connecting two settlements or two administrative districts, and they are considered primarily to be the responsibility of the territorial government. But here, too, depending upon the circumstances and merits of the case, the federal government may participate both in respect of capital cost in the first instance and the cost of maintenance in the second place.
The third classification is that of local roads. These are roads within settlements, such as roads within the administrative district of Yellowknife. They are the responsibility of the local administrative district.
